title: USB transmission gradually slowing down in a sawtooth pattern on Raspberry Pi Pico
body: I am using a Raspberry Pi Pico with MicroPython as a scientific data-acquisition platform. The Pico repeatedly writes byte data through usys.stdout.buffer.write(), while a Linux computer reads 10 kB chunks from /dev/ttyACM0. At 250 MHz, a 10 kB read initially takes about 0.015 seconds, but it gradually rises to roughly 0.05 seconds before suddenly returning to the fast rate; this sawtooth pattern repeats. At 125 MHz the speeds are roughly halved. The Pico does not reset, inserting a one-second pause does not reset the slowdown, micropython.mem_info() remains stable, and the measured Pico loop period follows the computer's receive time without apparent packet loss. I would like consistently high USB throughput.

symptoms_visible: Reading each 10 kB block from /dev/ttyACM0 initially takes about 0.015 seconds, then gradually takes around 0.05 seconds before suddenly becoming fast again.
The slowing and recovery repeat in a sawtooth pattern, while the Pico remains running and I do not observe packet loss.
N0.label: N0 repeating USB throughput slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: The USB transfer time repeatedly climbs and drops back down while the Pico surface remains below 35 °C.
N1.label: N1 thermal throttling evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After I create the bytes object once and reuse it, throughput improves by a few percent but still cycles with the same period, approximately every 418 chunks or 4180 kB.
N2_x.label: N2_x preallocated buffer aftermath

symptoms_visible: The same sawtooth remains on the newer MicroPython development firmware and on a different computer.
Explicitly collecting garbage in every write cycle adds a constant delay but does not remove the cycling.
Changing clock speed, computer read size, or Pico write size changes details of the curve, but the repeated slowdown remains.
N3.label: N3 firmware and workload probes completed

symptoms_visible: A standalone C program flooding USB through TinyUSB sustains about 770 kB/s without the MicroPython sawtooth.
A UART comparison has a different, much smaller periodic timing variation.
N4.label: N4 standalone TinyUSB comparison collected

symptoms_visible: With the candidate MicroPython build, the original Pico and PC scripts sustain about 7 Mbit/s and the sawtooth no longer appears.
N5.label: N5 candidate dependency update verified

symptoms_visible: On MicroPython firmware containing the updated RP2040 USB dependencies, Pico-to-PC transmission remains fast and the repeating sawtooth slowdown is gone.
N_terminal.label: terminal sustained USB throughput restored

question_patterns: Have you measured the Pico's temperature during the test?
Does the behavior become steadier without overclocking, and could thermal throttling be involved?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The Pico's surface temperature stays well below 35 °C throughout the test, even while overclocked, so I do not expect thermal throttling.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The chip becomes very hot, and the slowdown disappears when I run it at the standard clock under active cooling.
The measured surface temperature is around 32 °C instead of 35 °C, with the same sawtooth.

edges.comment: The reporter also posted the first plotted view of the sawtooth at this point; it is represented as volunteered information on N1.

solution.intent: Avoid allocating a new 10 kB object for every write by constructing the bytes buffer once and reusing it.
solution.concrete_example: Create data = b'x' * 10000 before the loop, then repeatedly call usys.stdout.buffer.write(data).

edges.comment: This real attempt improved throughput by only a few percent. The same sawtooth remained and repeated after approximately 4180 kB, so repeated allocation in the reporter's Python loop was not the resolution.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce this with the latest available MicroPython development firmware?
Please install the newest RP2 build and rerun the original transfer test.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried the newer MicroPython v1.16 development build and saw no change whatsoever. The sawtooth still repeats, including when I measure it on a different computer.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The latest development firmware has steady throughput and the sawtooth is completely gone.
The curve has a slightly different shape on the second computer, but the same repeated slowdown remains.

question_patterns: How does the curve compare at the standard 125 MHz clock and at 250 MHz?
Does the pattern scale with the Pico clock speed?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The delays are roughly doubled at 125 MHz, so the bottleneck appears to be on the Pico side. Some curve features remain at both clock speeds, although the pattern does not scale exactly with the clock.

question_patterns: Does changing the computer's serial read size alter the pattern?
Can you repeat the measurement with smaller receive chunks?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I changed the computer script to receive 1 kB chunks and normalized the times to 10 kB. It reveals finer structure, but the overall gradual slowdown is still obvious.

question_patterns: What happens if the Pico writes much smaller byte arrays?
Does the behavior depend on the size of each buffer.write call?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With writes of 13 bytes or less, the sawtooth repeats after fewer total bytes. Writes from about 14 to 30 bytes show a similar sawtooth to the large writes, although the steps disappear.

question_patterns: Does explicitly running garbage collection during every cycle change the slowdown?
Can you reuse a fixed buffer, call gc.collect() after every write, and report the timing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reused a fixed bytes object and called gc.collect() in every cycle. It only slows transmission by a constant amount; the speed cycling still occurs.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Calling gc.collect() at a fixed interval prevents the gradual slowdown and produces a steady transfer rate.

edges.comment: These are measurement probes. The version test changes the installed firmware to the then-current development build, while workload and garbage-collection tests collect evidence without supplying a lasting fix.

question_patterns: Can you repeat a comparable transfer over the RP2040 UART instead of USB?
Does a USB-to-UART adapter show the same gradual sawtooth?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Over UART, a 10000-byte block at 921600 baud oscillates between about 0.10767 and 0.1131 seconds, with a peak every six transmissions. Doubling the baud rate halves the time, and changing the block size does not change that pattern.

question_patterns: Can you run an equivalent USB flooding test outside MicroPython to narrow down which layer is involved?
Please try a simple compiled RP2040 USB CDC program and plot its sustained throughput.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I built a small Arduino C program based on the Adafruit TinyUSB CDC example and flooded Serial.printf(). It sustains about 770 kB/s with a flat curve and no sawtooth.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The standalone C TinyUSB program shows the same gradual sawtooth at the same transmitted-byte interval.
The standalone program sustains 730 kB/s rather than 770 kB/s, but its curve is still flat.

edges.comment: The UART result came from another affected participant and is folded into the simulated user side. The reporter supplied the standalone C/TinyUSB comparison, showing that TinyUSB could sustain high throughput in a different integration.

question_patterns: Can the original Pico and PC scripts be rerun with this candidate MicroPython build?
Please test the candidate build with the original reproduction and report whether the transfer curve remains steady.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reproduced the sawtooth with the original scripts, then ran the same test with the candidate build. That build sustains about 7 Mbit/s and the sawtooth is completely gone.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The candidate build still has the same sawtooth and reaches the same slow transfer times.
The candidate build sustains about 6.5 Mbit/s instead of 7 Mbit/s, with no sawtooth.

edges.comment: Pre-landing candidate-build measurement performed by a maintainer and folded into the user side. The raw outcome is sustained throughput; identifying the relevant dependency update as the accepted fix is engineer-side inference.

solution.intent: Update the RP2 MicroPython firmware to a build containing the newer bundled Pico SDK and TinyUSB revisions, which remove the repeating USB CDC throughput slowdown; retain sys.stdout.buffer.write for raw byte data.
solution.concrete_example: Build or install current RP2 MicroPython firmware containing the refreshed Pico SDK and TinyUSB dependencies, rerun the original 10 kB transfer test, and confirm that throughput remains near 7 Mbit/s without the sawtooth. Endpoint-buffer enlargement may improve peak throughput further, but it is not the underlying sawtooth fix.
solution.inference_hint: The candidate branch updated MicroPython's bundled Pico SDK and TinyUSB and eliminated the sawtooth. Maintainers explicitly did not bisect those upstream dependencies, so the accepted diagnosis must remain at that level: the issue was somewhere in the older Pico SDK and/or TinyUSB integration, not a precisely identified internal mechanism.

edges.comment: The dependency refresh was merged and maintainers declared the issue fully resolved. Later endpoint-size and print optimizations improved throughput but were separate from the accepted sawtooth resolution.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause at the level established by the thread: the sawtooth came from the older Pico SDK and/or TinyUSB revisions bundled with the RP2 MicroPython port; maintainers did not bisect the dependencies far enough to name a more precise mechanism.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: thermal throttling was absent, preallocating the Python buffer and forcing garbage collection did not remove the cycle, standalone C/TinyUSB sustained a flat transfer rate, and the candidate dependency update removed the sawtooth.
Must recommend using RP2 MicroPython firmware containing the updated Pico SDK and TinyUSB dependencies while using sys.stdout.buffer.write for raw bytes.

Must not present repeated Python allocation, heap garbage collection, or endpoint-buffer tuning alone as the root fix; buffer preallocation only improved speed slightly, explicit collection did not remove the cycle, and endpoint sizing was a separate throughput optimization.
Must ask the user to verify sustained throughput with the original reproduction on a build containing the dependency update before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable scientific user and hardware experimenter; comfortable with Python, serial-port scripts, oscilloscope measurements, firmware installation, clock changes, and compiling a small Arduino/TinyUSB comparison, but not comfortable debugging the MicroPython and TinyUSB internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, quantitative, curious, and cooperative; posts scripts and plots, tests hypotheses carefully, challenges explanations with counter-evidence, and openly states when a codebase is beyond available time or expertise.
